sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities advanced despite a bruising sovereign-bond sell-off, led by a powerful rebound in US mega-cap technology. MSCI World rose roughly **0.8%** (approx., verify before merging), with MSCI Developed Markets similar (approx., verify before merging) and MSCI Emerging Markets broadly flat (approx., verify before merging). The S&P 500 gained **1.1%** to **7,743.41**, while the MAG7 mega-cap tech cohort powered the Nasdaq up **3.2%** to a record **27,068.72**; the Dow lagged, slipping **0.28%** to **51,828.62**. Euro Stoxx 50 firmed about **0.5%** to **6,302.82**, China's CSI 300 eased **0.06%** to around **4,439**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell **0.2%** to **24,510**, and Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed roughly **2%** to **66,364**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities notched a winning week, though the gains were narrow and tech-led. The S&P 500 added **1.1%** to close at **7,743.41** and the Nasdaq surged **3.2%** to a record **27,068.72**, while the Dow shed **0.28%** to **51,828.62** despite a Friday jump of **0.93%** that snapped a three-week losing streak.

The dominant force was another volatile week for Treasuries: the 10-year UST yield touched **5.228%**, its highest since 2007, before easing to **5.16%** as Friday's oil pullback and prospective US-Iran diplomacy brought relief. Data stayed resilient, with the composite PMI jumping to **58.4**, a five-year high, core capital goods orders up **1.6%** and headline durable goods flat.

Style leadership favoured growth firmly over value, with semiconductors and mega-cap tech driving the tape while rate-sensitive and cyclical Dow names lagged. Elevated yields kept valuations in focus, yet investors rotated back into the AI complex as crude retreated late in the week.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities eked out a modest advance, with the STOXX Europe 600 rising about **0.5%** for its best week since early August and snapping a three-week losing streak. The Euro Stoxx 50 closed near **6,302.82**, the DAX added roughly **0.4%**, while the FTSE 100 and CAC 40 were more subdued.

The week's push and pull was clear: relief from falling oil eased fears of a fresh inflation shock from the Middle East, but rising bond yields capped the upside. With euro-area inflation running above **3%** and energy costs lifting government yields to multi-year highs, markets leaned towards a firmer ECB stance, limiting gains and driving notable dispersion across regions and sectors.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japanese equities led the region as markets reopened after the Silver Week holiday. The Nikkei 225 rose roughly **2%** to **66,364.20** and the TOPIX gained **1.31%** to **4,128.59**, buoyed by banks, whose sector index jumped **4.08%** on Friday, and semiconductors, with Tokyo Electron up **4.82%**. The move came even as the 10-year JGB yield hit **3.075%**, its highest since 1996.

China was mixed and quieter. The CSI 300 slipped **0.06%** and the Shanghai Composite rose **0.61%**, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng eased **0.22%**. Mainland shares outperformed Hong Kong after a technology-led rebound on Friday, as early weakness in AI and other growth names gave way to a sharp recovery in semiconductors.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar strengthened broadly as a higher-for-longer rates narrative gained traction, underpinned by rising UST yields and a composite PMI at a five-year high of **58.4**. The Japanese yen was the weakest major, with USD/JPY climbing to a three-week high as widening yield differentials continued to favour the dollar.

Risk sentiment soured for carry trades: USD/MXN rose about **2.6%** to near **17.67** as stronger US activity, higher yields and firmer oil triggered a broader emerging-market unwind. Among central banks, Norges Bank raised rates **25bps** to **4.50%**, while the SNB held at **0%**, the Riksbank at **1.75%** and Banxico at **6.50%**.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
The dominant theme was macro pressure meeting supply tightness, with the Bloomberg Commodity Index heading for its first weekly loss in four, down **0.8%** and trimming its year-to-date gain to **36%**. Brent traded near unchanged around **USD 105.4**, having swung within a range of more than **USD 10** on shifting Middle East supply and geopolitical signals, including talk of a phased US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Copper stayed resilient, with LME prices just **1%** below their recent record of **USD 14,875** per tonne and COMEX around **2%** below Monday's peak of **USD 6.9285** per pound, as physical tightness offset macro headwinds. Gold held its established **USD 4,300–4,400** range, with Fed expectations, yields and the dollar setting the near-term tone.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
It was a volatile week for sovereign bonds. The 10-year UST yield reached **5.228%**, its highest since 2007, before easing to close near **5.16%**, while the 2-year fell to **4.85%**, leaving the curve steeper as long-end supply and higher-for-longer pricing dominated. The 10-year yield has climbed more than **40bps** in September alone.

Stabilisation late in the week came from a pullback in oil and reports of prospective US-Iran diplomacy, which took some heat out of the sell-off. Globally, Japan's 10-year JGB yield hit **3.075%**, its highest since 1996. Despite the rate volatility, the equity rebound pointed to a resilient risk tone across IG and HY credit.
